items.prompt: What is the accessibility tree, and how does a generic <div> populate it compared to a semantic element like <button>?
choices: The accessibility tree is identical to the DOM tree; there's no real difference

A second structure the browser derives from the markup, read by screen readers and other assistive tech — semantic elements populate it with a correct role/name/state automatically, while a <div> populates it as generic, with no meaningful role
The accessibility tree only exists if a screen reader is actively installed on the machine
A <div> gets the same role as a <button> automatically, since both are HTML elements
items.explanation: The accessibility tree is a parallel structure specifically for non-visual/non-mouse interaction. Semantic elements carry inherent role/name/state information into it; a <div> has no inherent role, so its entry is essentially empty regardless of how it looks visually.

items.prompt: A <div onclick="..."> is styled to look exactly like a button. Which of these does it NOT get for free, unlike a real <button>?
choices: Its visual appearance (already handled by CSS)
The ability to have an onclick handler at all
The ability to be clicked with a mouse
items.explanation: Mouse clicking and visual styling work identically either way — the gap is specifically keyboard behavior: a <div> isn't focusable or Enter/Space-activatable by default, and reproducing that requires manual tabindex and keydown handling.

items.prompt: Why can't a screen reader user "jump directly to the main content" on a page built entirely out of <div>s, even if it's visually laid out with a clear header/nav/content structure?
choices: Screen readers can't detect visual layout at all, regardless of markup
The 'jump to landmark' capability depends on real landmark elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>) being present in the markup — a <div>-only page has no landmarks to jump between, no matter how it looks
Landmarks only work if the page has no CSS applied
This is a browser limitation, not an HTML one, and applies even to semantic pages
items.explanation: The landmark-jumping shortcut is a real assistive-technology feature that depends specifically on semantic landmark tags being present — visual structure achieved purely through CSS on <div>s carries no equivalent signal for a screen reader to jump between.

items.prompt: A developer adds role="button" to a <div onclick="..."> but adds nothing else. Per L3's failure modes, is the div now fully accessible?
choices: Yes — role="button" makes it functionally identical to a real <button>
No — role="button" only fixes the announced accessibility-tree role; the div still isn't keyboard-focusable and won't respond to Enter/Space unless tabindex and a keydown handler are also added
No, because role attributes are purely decorative and have no effect at all
Yes, as long as the div also has an onclick handler
items.explanation: All three pieces — correct role, focusability, keyboard activation — have to be present together. role="button" alone only addresses the announced role; a native <button> has all three by construction, which is exactly why it's simpler than manually assembling the equivalent.

items.prompt: Implement `isKeyboardAccessible(el)` from L3: `el` is `{ tag, href?, tabIndex?, hasKeyHandler? }`. Native interactive tags (button, input, select, textarea) are always accessible; an `a` tag is only accessible if it has a non-empty `href`; any other tag is only accessible if it has BOTH `tabIndex === 0` AND `hasKeyHandler === true`.

tests.description: a link with an href is accessible
a link with no href is NOT accessible
a bare div with an onclick-style handler is not accessible
a div with only tabIndex (no key handler) is still not accessible
a div with both tabIndex and a key handler is accessible

items.explanation: This encodes the real rule browsers apply: most native interactive elements are unconditionally accessible, `a` depends on actually being a link (a real href), and anything else only counts if BOTH the focus stop and the key handling were added by hand — missing either one leaves it broken for keyboard users, which is exactly the gap that makes native elements simpler than reimplementing them.
